data.title: Choose the correct answer for each question.
data.description: Practise distinctions between the Present Perfect Simple and Continuous, focusing on duration, repeated activity, result and completion.
learningPoints: Use the Present Perfect Continuous to emphasise duration or ongoing activity.
Use the Present Perfect Simple to emphasise completion, result or quantity.
Recognise stative verbs that are not normally used in continuous forms.
Use for and since accurately with continuing situations.
Distinguish repeated activity from completed achievement.
Choose aspect according to whether the focus is process or result.

sections.explain: Use HAVE/HAS BEEN + verb-ing when the focus is on how long an activity has continued.

words.word: I've been studying for three hours.
I've studied for three hours and I'm still in the middle of it, with focus only on process.
I've been study for three hours.

sections.summary: Choosing simple aspect for completed quantity.
sections.explain: Use the Present Perfect Simple when the focus is on a completed amount or number.

words.word: I've written five emails this morning.
I've been writing five emails this morning, and all five are complete.
I've wrote five emails this morning.

sections.summary: Using continuous aspect for recent visible evidence.
sections.explain: The Present Perfect Continuous often explains a present result from a recent activity.

words.word: You're wet. Have you been walking in the rain?
You're wet. Have you walked in the rain continuously until now as a completed result?
You're wet. Have you been walked in the rain?

sections.summary: Avoiding continuous forms with stative verbs.
sections.explain: Stative verbs such as KNOW are not normally used in continuous perfect forms.

words.word: I've known her for years.
I've been knowing her for years.
I've knew her for years.

sections.explain: Use continuous aspect for the activity and simple aspect for its completed result.

words.word: I've been painting the kitchen, but I haven't finished it yet.
I've painted the kitchen, but I haven't finished it yet, with clear completed-result meaning.
I've been painted the kitchen, but I haven't finished it yet.

sections.explain: A completed achievement is usually expressed with the Present Perfect Simple.

words.word: She has finally passed her driving test.
She has finally been passing her driving test.
She has finally pass her driving test.

sections.summary: Using continuous aspect for repeated activity.
sections.explain: The Present Perfect Continuous can emphasise repeated activity over a period up to now.

words.word: They've been calling me all morning.
They've called me all morning, with the focus clearly on the ongoing repeated process.
They've been called me all morning.

sections.explain: Questions about completed quantity normally use the Present Perfect Simple.

words.word: How many books have you read this year?
How many books have you been reading this year, if you mean the completed total?
How many books have you readed this year?

sections.explain: HOW LONG often combines naturally with the Present Perfect Continuous for ongoing activities.

words.word: How long have you been waiting?
How long have you waited, if the waiting is still continuing and duration is the focus?
How long have you been waited?

sections.explain: Simple aspect highlights result; continuous aspect highlights process.

words.word: I've repaired the bike, so you can use it now.
I've been repairing the bike, so the completed repair is definitely the focus.
I've repair the bike, so you can use it now.
